analysis.one_liner: Lets regulators fine insurers and benefit administrators that illegally shortchange mental health coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in December 2024 and referred to committee, where it died without a hearing or vote as the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already requires health plans to cover mental health and substance use care on the same terms as physical care, but there is little penalty for breaking that rule. This bill would let the federal government impose civil money penalties on plans that violate parity—and, importantly, it would also hold the outside companies that actually run benefits (third-party administrators, behavioral health managers, and pharmacy benefit managers) liable when they cause a violation. It never received a committee hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People with mental health or substance use conditions covered by employer or individual insurance plans. Under current law, federal regulators have had weak financial leverage to punish plans that make mental health coverage harder to use than medical coverage; the bill would add civil monetary penalties and spread liability to the administrators and pharmacy benefit managers that often make the actual coverage decisions. States would also gain a clearer enforcement role.

how_it_helps.text: Federal law already requires health plans to cover mental health and substance use care on equal terms with physical care; the bill adds civil money penalties as an enforcement tool when plans fail to do so.

It extends liability beyond the insurance company to the third parties that actually administer benefits—including third-party administrators, managed behavioral health organizations, and pharmacy benefit managers—closing a path plans use to push responsibility onto vendors.
It lets states enforce parity requirements against plan sponsors and service providers, adding more enforcers.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, employers that sponsor plans, and the third-party companies that administer behavioral health and pharmacy benefits, who would face fines and compliance costs when parity rules are violated.

drawbacks.text: Penalties could raise costs for employers who sponsor health plans, and some of that cost could be passed to workers through premiums.

The bill gives the Secretary discretion to divide liability percentages between plans, sponsors, and service providers, which could invite litigation over how responsibility is apportioned after a violation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: federal audits and investigations have found many health plans restrict mental health care more tightly than physical care, and meaningful penalties are the missing lever to make existing parity law bite. The costs are modest and legitimate—compliance work for insurers and the companies that run their benefits, and some risk that plans respond by trimming mental health offerings or raising premiums to manage penalty exposure. On balance, the policy addresses a widely acknowledged enforcement gap, though it died before any scrutiny or refinement.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate health committee in December 2024, and the Congress ended before the committee or the Senate ever took it up.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Murphy introduced the Parity Enforcement Act of 2024 on December 12, 2024.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day.
No further action was taken; the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.
It had two Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support on the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers, employers, and benefit administrators keep facing no federal fines for parity violations, so people who are denied equal mental health coverage remain without that remedy.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and benefits administrators; no parity penalties

for.name: Sen. Chris Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its push for enforceable penalties on parity violations.

for.name: Sens. Tina Smith and Ben Ray Luján

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only on-record support was three Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and no one opposed it on the record because it never advanced to a vote.

industries.industry: Health insurers and group health plans
industries.note: They become directly liable to civil penalties for violating mental health parity rules, which many plans have been found to violate. Consumers gain an enforcement mechanism that currently lacks teeth.

industries.industry: Third-party administrators and behavioral health utilization-review firms
industries.note: Companies that manage behavioral health benefits on insurers' behalf would share liability for parity violations they cause, changing how they review and restrict mental health claims.
PBMs would be liable for parity violations in drug benefits they administer, such as unequal coverage for mental health medications.
